paras: The threatened lynching of Anthony Cantieny took place at the Minneapolis jail around March 1885, during his trial for killing a police officer, when talk of lynching led the mayor to order out the military. Nobody was hurt, and Cantieny was convicted of manslaughter. It is known only from a St. Paul Daily Globe column of November 1888, which gave two versions of the threat.

Cantieny, a young man, killed Minneapolis Patrolman McLaughlin after an altercation while he had been "on a spree". According to the Globe's 1888 comment, McLaughlin fired first as Cantieny tried to escape arrest for disorderly conduct, and Cantieny fired back.

At the time of the trial, the Globe recalled, "there was some talk of lynching Cantieny," and Mayor Pillsbury ordered the military out to guard the jail. Jacob Hein, then a police sergeant and captain of a local military company, refused the order and was dismissed from the police force. About half a dozen policemen under Chief West guarded the jail. Col. Bend marched militia loaded with ball to within a couple of blocks of the jail, but nobody was hurt.

Cantieny was convicted of manslaughter on March 28, 1885 and sentenced to seven years in the state prison. In November 1888 Gov. McGill pardoned him on the recommendation of, among others, the jury, former chief West and Hein, by then superintendent of police.

No contemporary account of the crowd appears in the coverage; the Globe raised it in a Minneapolis "Current Comment" column on November 30, 1888, as police officers criticized Hein for signing the pardon petition, while its pardon reports of the two previous days did not mention it. The column presented the lynching story as a statement "going the rounds" to illustrate that "time works wonders," since Hein had once refused to protect "the murderer of a brother officer."

The same column offered a second version in which Hein objected only to sending armed men against "a mob (?) of boys and men" who could not have entered the jail. In this telling the crowd was "boys and curiosity seekers" whose presence was not "even a menace" of a lynching.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Anthony Cantieny
bases: A crowd gathered at the Minneapolis jail amid 'talk of lynching' a prisoner on trial for killing a policeman, and the mayor ordered the military out to guard the jail; no one was harmed (A4).

No one was killed: the crowd at the jail did not reach Cantieny and 'nobody was hurt' (A4); the crowd's size is not given, and its pretext was the killing of a police officer, for which Cantieny was later convicted of manslaughter (A2, A4).

The threat is known only from one retrospective column in the St. Paul Daily Globe, written more than three years later, which itself gives two versions of how serious the crowd was (A4); the pardon reports (A2, A3) do not mention it.

accounts.label: Story 'going the rounds' (1888)
accounts.gist: There was talk of lynching Cantieny; Mayor Pillsbury ordered the military out, and Hein, angry at the 'murderer of a brother officer', refused to lead his company and was dismissed.

accounts.label: Second version in the same column
accounts.gist: Hein refused because he thought it folly to send armed men against boys and men who could not have entered the jail; six policemen were enough, Chief West's coolness kept anyone from being hurt, and the crowd was not 'even a menace' of a lynching.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Daily Globe's Minneapolis 'Current Comment' repeats the lynching story as an anecdote about Hein, then calls the crowd 'a mob (?)' of 'boys and curiosity seekers' and blames Col. Bend for being 'anxious to shoot into the crowd'.

versions.value: There was talk of lynching, serious enough that the mayor called out the military to guard the jail
The crowd was boys and curiosity seekers who could not have entered the jail and were not even a menace

conflicts.note: Both versions appear in one 1888 column, written more than three years later; neither is attributed to a named source, and no contemporary report of the crowd was found.
